cloze.text: {{c1::Agranulocytosis}} is acquired (due to drugs, autoimmune conditions or bone marrow failure), whereas {{c2::cyclic neutropenia}} is caused by a genetic mutation affecting bone marrow regulation.
Symptoms of agranulocytosis (and, the same, of cyclic neutropenia): {{c1::fever}}, malaise, {{c2::sore throat}}, skin infections and {{c3::oral ulcers}}.
Oral impact of agranulocytosis: {{c1::ulcerations}}, {{c2::periodontal destruction}} with attachment loss, delayed healing and infections.
In cyclic neutropenia the oral problems (same as agranulocytosis) {{c1::worsen during the neutropenic phase}} and {{c2::improve when the neutrophil count returns to normal}}.
Dental care in agranulocytosis: use {{c1::preventive antibiotics}}, gentle hygiene and {{c2::antimicrobial rinses}}; schedule care during {{c3::stable neutrophil periods}}.
cloze.extra: Why: oral ulcers, rapid attachment loss and gingival breakdown.

cloze.text: Dental care in cyclic neutropenia: same as agranulocytosis, and {{c1::delay care during low neutrophil counts}}.

Agranulocytosis and cyclic neutropenia both involve dangerously low levels of {{c1::neutrophils}}, a type of {{c2::white blood cell (granulocyte)}} essential for fighting infection, especially in the oral cavity.
{{c1::Cerebral palsy}} is a disorder caused by brain development issues before or shortly after birth, affecting {{c2::muscle control and coordination}}.
Cause of cerebral palsy: brain injury or abnormal development, often {{c1::before birth}} (e.g., {{c2::lack of oxygen}}, infection or trauma).
Signs of cerebral palsy: {{c1::involuntary or stiff movements}}, poor balance, and difficulty with posture or coordination.
Most patients with cerebral palsy have {{c1::normal intelligence}}; learning difficulties may be due to {{c2::vision or hearing impairment}}, not intellectual disability.
Cerebral palsy, dental: {{c1::drooling}}, a strong {{c2::gag reflex}} and trouble opening the mouth (muscle dysfunction).
In cerebral palsy, gingival hyperplasia can result from seizure medications such as {{c1::phenytoin}}.
Cerebral palsy, dental: {{c1::bruxism}}, attrition, and trauma from falls or uncontrolled movement.
Cerebral palsy, dental: mouth breathing, {{c1::tongue thrusting}} and {{c2::TMJ}} problems.
Patients with cerebral palsy are at high risk for {{c1::caries and periodontal disease}} because of difficulty with home care.
{{c1::Spinal cord injury}}: damage to the spinal cord that results in loss of mobility or function {{c2::below the level of injury}}.
In spinal cord injury, the {{c1::higher}} the injury, the more severe the paralysis and disability.
Spinal cord injury at {{c1::C2–C3}}: minimal head/neck movement; the patient depends on a {{c2::ventilator}}.
Spinal cord injury at C4: arm and leg paralysis; possible {{c1::breathing difficulty}}.
Spinal cord injury at C5: limited {{c1::shoulder}} control; needs {{c2::adaptive aids}} for oral care.
Spinal cord injury at C7: functional hand and arm movement; the patient may perform {{c1::self-care}}.
Spinal cord injury at T1–T12: full {{c1::upper body}} function, increased rib and trunk control; may use a wheelchair or crutches {{c2::independently}}.
Spinal cord injury, dental: schedule appointments with {{c1::extra time}} for positioning, transfers and comfort; use {{c2::tilting wheelchair-compatible chairs}} when possible.
Spinal cord injury, dental: encourage {{c1::adaptive oral hygiene aids}} (e.g., floss holders, electric toothbrushes).
{{c1::Spina bifida}} is a {{c2::neural tube defect}} in which the spine does not close properly during early pregnancy, leading to incomplete development of the brain or spinal cord.
Spina bifida is linked to {{c1::folic acid (vitamin B9)}} deficiency during the {{c2::first month}} of pregnancy.
{{c1::Meningocele}}: the meninges and cerebrospinal fluid protrude through a spinal opening; it can cause {{c2::hydrocephalus}} (excess fluid in the brain).
Severity of spina bifida ranges from mild weakness to permanent paralysis, depending on the {{c1::location and type}}.
Spina bifida, dental: always ask about a {{c1::latex allergy}}; some patients have {{c2::shunts}} or other medical devices.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Cause of muscular dystrophy: a {{c1::genetic defect}} causing progressive muscle fiber degeneration.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Cause of ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis): neurodegeneration that kills {{c1::motor neurons}}, not brain cells.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Cause of multiple sclerosis: autoimmune attack on the {{c1::myelin sheath}} of nerves.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Cause of myasthenia gravis: autoimmune attack on the {{c1::nerve-muscle connection}} ({{c2::ACh receptors}}).

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Onset of myasthenia gravis is variable — often {{c1::women under 40}} and {{c2::men over 60}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Progression of muscular dystrophy: gradual muscle weakness, starting in the {{c1::lower body}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Progression of ALS: {{c1::rapid}} loss of voluntary muscle control; {{c2::breathing}} becomes affected.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: ALS = motor neuron death → progressive paralysis with NO remission; MS = damage to nerve insulation (myelin) → unpredictable flare-ups and remissions. In both the mind remains intact.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Progression of multiple sclerosis: a {{c1::flare/remission}} pattern with gradual worsening.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: In myasthenia gravis weakness fluctuates daily — it {{c1::worsens with exertion}} and {{c2::improves with rest}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Cognition is normal in muscular dystrophy, ALS and myasthenia gravis; in multiple sclerosis it is usually intact but may affect {{c1::focus/memory}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Mobility: in ALS a {{c1::wheelchair}} is often required; in MS it varies — {{c2::cane, walker or wheelchair}} over time.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: In myasthenia gravis, weakness affects walking, {{c1::chewing}}, speaking and {{c2::breathing}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Muscular dystrophy, dental: the patient needs help with oral hygiene; treat in an {{c1::upright/semi-upright}} position.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: ALS, dental: needs help with oral hygiene, treat upright; monitor {{c1::swallowing}} and {{c2::aspiration}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Multiple sclerosis, dental: avoid {{c1::overheating}}; manage {{c2::spasms}}.

cloze.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
cloze.text: Myasthenia gravis, dental: {{c1::short, morning}} visits; avoid {{c2::fatigue}}; monitor breathing and swallowing.
{{c1::Marfan syndrome}} is a genetic disorder of the body's {{c2::connective tissue}}, leading to problems with the skeleton, eyes, blood vessels and heart.
Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in genes that control {{c1::fibrillin}}, a protein that helps form elastic fibers in connective tissue.
Marfan syndrome signs: usually very {{c1::tall and thin}}, with long fingers and flexible joints, and heart complications like {{c2::aortic aneurysm}}.
Marfan syndrome, dental: {{c1::high-arched palate}}, narrow jaw and crowded teeth increase caries risk; {{c2::malocclusion}} is common and may require orthodontic care.
Marfan syndrome with heart involvement: consult the physician — antibiotic premedication only if the patient meets the {{c1::AHA 2021}} criteria (e.g., a {{c2::prosthetic/replaced heart valve}}).
cloze.extra: Exam standard (AHA 2021) beats the book: the book says heart involvement 'may require premedication'. Prophylaxis is only for prosthetic valves or valve-repair material, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and cardiac transplant with valvulopathy — Marfan syndrome or aortic aneurysm alone is not an indication.

cloze.text: Rheumatoid arthritis is {{c1::autoimmune}} — it attacks the joint lining ({{c2::synovium}}).
Osteoarthritis is {{c1::wear and tear}} — breakdown of joint {{c2::cartilage}}.
Pattern: rheumatoid arthritis is {{c1::symmetrical}} (both sides of the body); osteoarthritis is {{c2::asymmetrical}} (usually one side worsens first).
Age of onset: rheumatoid arthritis can begin in {{c1::young adults}}; osteoarthritis usually affects {{c2::older adults}}.
Inflammation: in rheumatoid arthritis joints are {{c1::warm, swollen and painful}}; osteoarthritis has less inflammation and more {{c2::grinding and stiffness}}.
Rheumatoid arthritis, dental: TMJ pain; {{c1::aspirin}} → bleeding risk; {{c2::corticosteroids}} → delayed healing and infection risk.
Osteoarthritis, dental: TMJ {{c1::stiffness}} and limited opening.

Board Alert: keywords such as seniors, arthritis, mobility issues or muscular disorders → think {{c1::electric toothbrush, power flossers}} and other tools that help someone who cannot use their hands properly for oral hygiene.
Body weight: anorexia nervosa — {{c1::underweight}} (significantly below the healthy range); bulimia nervosa — often {{c2::normal weight or slightly overweight}}.
cloze.extra: The book prints the Body Weight row twice in this table.

cloze.text: Behavior: anorexia — intense fear of gaining weight and {{c1::refusal to eat}}; bulimia — eats large amounts, then {{c2::induces vomiting or uses laxatives}}.
Oral signs of anorexia nervosa: nutritional deficiency, {{c1::dry mouth}} and {{c2::angular cheilitis}}.
Oral signs of bulimia nervosa: {{c1::perimylolysis}} (acid erosion on the {{c2::linguals of the maxillary teeth}}), palatal trauma and {{c3::parotid enlargement}}.
cloze.extra: Book spells it 'perimolysis'. Photo in the book: erosion.

cloze.text: Common deficiencies: anorexia — iron, calcium, vitamin B, possible {{c1::osteoporosis}}; bulimia — {{c2::electrolyte imbalance}}, low pH, dehydration.
Anorexia, dental: {{c1::fluoride and remineralization}}; monitor erosion, caries and sensitivity.
Bulimia, dental: {{c1::avoid brushing right after vomiting}}; use non-acidic rinses; watch for soft tissue trauma and gland swelling; {{c2::refer}} if purging is suspected.
After vomiting, rinse gently with {{c1::water or a baking soda solution}} to neutralize the acid, because brushing too soon can {{c2::scrub away acid-softened enamel}}.
GERD: acid from the stomach flows backward into the {{c1::esophagus}}, causing irritation.
Peptic ulcer disease: open sores that develop in the lining of the {{c1::stomach or duodenum}}.
Cause of GERD: a weak {{c1::lower esophageal sphincter}}, worsened by spicy foods, caffeine and obesity.
Cause of peptic ulcer disease: {{c1::Helicobacter pylori}} infection, or {{c2::NSAIDs}} like aspirin or ibuprofen.
Symptoms: GERD — heartburn, especially {{c1::when lying down}}; peptic ulcer — heartburn, nausea, bloating, sometimes {{c2::vomiting blood}}.
Oral signs of GERD: enamel erosion on the {{c1::linguals of the maxillary teeth}}, sensitive teeth and bad breath.
Oral signs of peptic ulcer disease: possible bad breath and {{c1::dry mouth from medication}}.
GERD, dental: avoid acidic products and rinses; recommend fluoride and remineralization; schedule {{c1::upright}} appointments.
Peptic ulcer disease, dental: avoid aspirin when possible; expect {{c1::delayed healing}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Celiac disease: an autoimmune reaction to {{c1::gluten}} that damages the {{c2::small intestine lining}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Crohn's disease: chronic inflammatory disease affecting {{c1::any part of the GI tract}} (mouth to anus).
cloze.extra: The book's figure on p.219 swaps the two inflammation labels; the table (and this card) are correct.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Ulcerative colitis: chronic inflammation of the {{c1::colon and rectum only}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Celiac disease is triggered by gluten in {{c1::wheat, barley and rye}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Cause of Crohn's disease: {{c1::unknown}} — likely immune-related with genetic/environmental triggers; ulcerative colitis is similar (immune-mediated, colon-specific inflammation).

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Oral signs of celiac disease: {{c1::glossitis}}, aphthous ulcers and {{c2::enamel defects}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Oral signs of Crohn's disease: oral ulcers and a {{c1::cobblestone}} appearance of the buccal mucosa.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Oral signs of ulcerative colitis: oral ulcers and mucosal inflammation, {{c1::less severe}} than in Crohn's.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Symptoms: celiac — diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, {{c1::nutrient malabsorption}}; Crohn's — cramping, diarrhea, weight loss, possible {{c2::perianal disease}}; ulcerative colitis — {{c3::bloody diarrhea}}, urgency, abdominal pain.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Celiac disease, dental: monitor for ulcers and nutrient deficiencies; recommend {{c1::gluten-free}} home care if needed; assess healing and medication impact.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Crohn's disease, dental: watch for ulcers, dehydration, {{c1::steroid use}} and delayed healing; schedule around {{c2::flare-ups}}.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: Ulcerative colitis, dental: similar to Crohn's; assess {{c1::bleeding risk}}, fatigue and healing delay.

cloze.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
cloze.text: In celiac disease even small amounts of gluten — including in {{c1::toothpaste or mouth rinse}} — can trigger an autoimmune reaction; some contain gluten-derived ingredients used as {{c2::flavoring agents, binders or thickeners}}.
COPD is a chronic, {{c1::irreversible}} airflow limitation; asthma is a chronic inflammatory airway disease with {{c2::reversible}} obstruction.
cloze.extra: Progression: COPD = gradual worsening, irreversible; asthma = comes in attacks, generally reversible.

cloze.text: Cause: COPD — mainly {{c1::smoking}} or long-term exposure to irritants; asthma — triggered by {{c2::allergens}}, stress, cold air or exercise.
In COPD, long-term exposure damages lung tissue, thickens airways and {{c1::destroys alveoli}} (especially in emphysema), making {{c2::exhalation}} difficult.
In asthma, inflammation causes airway {{c1::swelling}} and {{c2::constriction of smooth muscles}}; excess mucus can also narrow the airway.
cloze.extra: Asthma: no structural damage — airway constriction with triggers.

cloze.text: Symptoms: COPD — persistent cough, sputum, shortness of breath, {{c1::barrel chest}} (emphysema); asthma — {{c2::wheezing}}, tight chest, episodic shortness of breath, coughing.
Medications: COPD — bronchodilators, steroids, {{c1::oxygen therapy}}; asthma — inhalers (e.g., {{c2::albuterol}}), corticosteroids.
COPD, dental: avoid {{c1::nitrous oxide}}; upright chair; monitor dry mouth and fatigue; avoid the {{c2::air polisher}}.
Asthma, dental: avoid {{c1::sulfites}}; the patient brings their {{c2::rescue inhaler}}; short appointments; upright chair.
{{c1::Cystic fibrosis}} is a genetic disorder causing thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs, digestive tract and {{c2::salivary glands}}, leading to respiratory and nutritional problems.
Cystic fibrosis is caused by an inherited mutation of the {{c1::CFTR}} gene.
Symptoms of cystic fibrosis: chronic cough, lung infections, {{c1::salty skin}}, poor growth, malabsorption and GI issues.
Oral signs of cystic fibrosis: {{c1::xerostomia}}, high caries risk, possibly enlarged salivary glands and {{c2::delayed dental development}}.
Cystic fibrosis, dental: delay care if an {{c1::active respiratory infection}} is present; use precautions to reduce {{c2::aerosol}} exposure; position the chair to support easier breathing.

basic.front: Why do patients with spina bifida often develop a latex allergy?
basic.back: They undergo multiple surgeries and medical procedures early in life, exposing them to latex before the immune system is fully developed; repeated contact raises the chance of a severe allergic reaction.

basic.front: Why is aspirin best avoided in patients with active or past peptic ulcers?
basic.back: It blocks protective prostaglandins in the stomach lining (worsening or triggering ulcers) and increases the risk of bleeding.

basic.extra: WakeUpMemory: "B" for Bronchitis — Blue, Bloated, Blocked Bronchi.

basic.back: Emphysema — alveolar damage and air trapping

mcq.question: A patient with cyclic neutropenia needs scaling and root planing. Which plan is best?
options: A. Treat at the low point of the neutrophil cycle, when gingival symptoms are most obvious
B. Schedule treatment when the neutrophil count has returned to normal
C. Treat at any time, because cyclic neutropenia does not affect the mouth
D. Avoid all antimicrobial rinses during treatment
mcq.answer: B. Schedule treatment when the neutrophil count has returned to normal
mcq.explanation: Cyclic neutropenia: oral problems worsen in the neutropenic phase, so care is delayed during low neutrophil counts and done when counts are normal. A is the opposite: infection risk is highest at the low point.

mcq.question: All of the following are typical dental findings in a patient with cerebral palsy EXCEPT:
options: A. Drooling
B. Gingival hyperplasia from phenytoin
C. Bruxism and attrition
D. A diminished gag reflex
mcq.explanation: The book lists a STRONG gag reflex (with drooling and trouble opening the mouth) in cerebral palsy. Phenytoin-induced gingival hyperplasia is typical because many patients take seizure medication.

mcq.question: A 14-year-old with spina bifida and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt arrives for a prophylaxis. Which question is MOST important at the medical history review?
options: A. Is there a history of latex allergy?
B. Is there a family history of cyclic neutropenia?
C. Does the patient grind their teeth at night?
D. Does the patient take phenytoin?
mcq.answer: A. Is there a history of latex allergy?
mcq.explanation: Latex allergy is common in spina bifida (many early surgeries mean early, repeated latex exposure) and can cause a severe reaction, so always ask. Phenytoin is a cerebral palsy/seizure concern, not specific to spina bifida.

mcq.section: Muscular dystrophy, ALS, MS, myasthenia gravis
mcq.question: A patient says her jaw muscles tire while chewing, the weakness gets worse as the day goes on, and it improves after rest. Which appointment plan is MOST appropriate?
options: A. Short morning appointments, avoiding fatigue
B. Long late-afternoon appointments to complete all treatment at once
C. Keep the operatory warm and the patient supine
D. No modification; cognition is normal so no special care is needed
mcq.answer: A. Short morning appointments, avoiding fatigue
mcq.explanation: Weakness that worsens with exertion and improves with rest = myasthenia gravis; schedule short morning visits, avoid fatigue, and monitor breathing and swallowing. Long afternoon visits catch the patient at her weakest.

mcq.question: A 35-year-old woman has warm, swollen, painful joints on both hands and takes daily aspirin and a corticosteroid. Which dental consideration is MOST important?
options: A. Increased bleeding risk and delayed healing/infection risk
B. Severe TMJ stiffness from cartilage wear
C. Perimylolysis from acid exposure
D. Latex allergy from early surgeries
mcq.answer: A. Increased bleeding risk and delayed healing/infection risk
mcq.explanation: Symmetrical, inflamed joints in a young adult = rheumatoid arthritis; aspirin raises bleeding risk and corticosteroids delay healing and raise infection risk. TMJ stiffness from cartilage wear describes osteoarthritis.

mcq.question: A 19-year-old of normal weight has smooth erosion on the lingual surfaces of the maxillary teeth, palatal trauma and bilateral parotid enlargement. Which condition is MOST likely?
options: A. Bulimia nervosa
B. Anorexia nervosa
C. GERD
D. Peptic ulcer disease
mcq.explanation: Perimylolysis + palatal trauma + parotid enlargement in a normal-weight patient = bulimia. GERD also erodes maxillary linguals but does not cause parotid enlargement; anorexia patients are underweight.

mcq.section: Celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis
mcq.question: A patient has cobblestone-like buccal mucosa, oral ulcers, cramping, weight loss and perianal disease. Which condition is MOST likely?
options: A. Crohn's disease
B. Ulcerative colitis
C. Celiac disease
D. Peptic ulcer disease
mcq.explanation: Cobblestone buccal mucosa and perianal disease point to Crohn's, which can affect any part of the GI tract. Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum and its oral signs are milder.

mcq.question: A 68-year-old long-time smoker with emphysema, barrel chest and chronic shortness of breath needs periodontal debridement. Which is contraindicated?
options: A. Nitrous oxide sedation
B. Seating the patient upright
C. Monitoring for dry mouth and fatigue
D. Using hand instruments instead of the air polisher
mcq.explanation: The book lists avoiding nitrous oxide (with upright positioning and avoiding the air polisher) for COPD. B, C and D are the recommended modifications.
